title: Emphasis: cleft sentences and basic inversion
tagline: Fronting, inversion and agreement: how English puts the important word first.
exam: Reading & Use of English Part 4 — key word transformations
Speaking Part 3 — collaborative task: making a point stand out
Writing Part 2 — essay: a confident, varied style
why: Standard word order tells a story in a flat, neutral voice. Emphatic structures let you highlight exactly which word matters — who did something, what you actually need, how rarely it happens — and B2 First rewards that control directly in Part 4 transformations, and less directly whenever an examiner notices a more confident style.

diagrams.title: Cleft sentence: moving the focus to the front

before.text: Sofia found the solution to the problem.

after.text: It was Sofia who found the solution to the problem.

steps: Identify the part you want to emphasise (Sofia).
Add 'who' for people or 'that' for things, then the rest of the sentence.

diagrams.title: Inversion after a negative or restrictive adverb

before.text: Miss Vega rarely gives extra homework.

after.text: Rarely does Miss Vega give extra homework.

steps: Move the adverb (Rarely) to the front of the sentence.
Add the auxiliary that matches the tense (does, for present simple) before the subject.
Put the main verb back in its base form: gives → give.

diagrams.title: Agreeing with so, neither and nor
diagrams.caption: Liam loves hiking. So does Nadia. — Mateo hasn't finished. Neither has Sofia.

head: Pattern
Structure
Example
rows: What Sofia wants is a fair result.
It was Liam who forgot the tickets.
The reason we're late is that the bus broke down.
Not only + inverted clause, but + subject + also + verb
Not only did she win, but she also broke the record.
Rarely does Miss Vega cancel a class.
Liam loves football. So do I.
Sofia hasn't finished. Neither have I.

use.point: Emphasising who or what is responsible for something

examples.text: It was Nadia who suggested filming the whole trip for the school channel.
What really impressed the judges was how calmly the team answered questions.
examples.note: what-cleft: the cause of the reaction

examples.text: What we need now is a proper plan, not more meetings.

use.point: Explaining a reason without starting every sentence with 'because'

examples.text: The reason we're behind schedule is that the printer broke down twice.
The reason why Sofia chose Arequipa for the exchange is the volcano-watching club there.

use.point: Adding force with not only... but also, and negative inversion

examples.text: Not only did the choir win first prize, but they also got invited to perform in Lima.
Never have the judges given a score that high before.
Rarely does Miss Vega let a class run over time, so something must be wrong.

use.point: Agreeing quickly with so, neither and nor

examples.text: Liam can't stand horror films. Neither can Sofia.
Mateo loves early morning training. So does Nadia.
I haven't finished the reading yet. Nor has Liam.
examples.note: negative agreement, nor instead of neither

watch_out.wrong: Not only she won the race, but also broke the record.
watch_out.right: Not only did she win the race, but she also broke the record.
watch_out.why: 'Not only' at the front triggers auxiliary inversion, and 'but also' still needs its own subject.

watch_out.wrong: Never I have seen such dedication.
watch_out.why: The order after a fronted negative adverb is adverb + auxiliary + subject, not adverb + subject + auxiliary.
After 'so', the auxiliary comes before the subject — that inversion is what shows agreement.
Neither and nor already carry the negative meaning, so don't add another negative auxiliary like 'don't'.

watch_out.wrong: It was Sofia which found the mistake.
watch_out.right: It was Sofia who found the mistake.
watch_out.why: Use 'who' for people in it-clefts; 'that' or 'which' are for things.

watch_out.wrong: What I need it's more practice.
watch_out.why: 'What I need' is already the subject of the sentence — don't add a second subject like 'it'.

dialogue.title: Sports Day record
dialogue.context: Liam, Sofia and Nadia are talking after Sports Day, where Nadia broke a school record, and Miss Vega joins them.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Did you hear? It was Nadia who broke the school record in the 200 metres.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Really? Not only did she win, but she also beat her own personal best.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Never have I seen her run that fast before.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: What surprised me most was how calm she looked at the finish line.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Thanks. Honestly, the reason I ran so well is that the whole team was cheering.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: I was shouting myself hoarse. So was Miss Vega, actually.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: I certainly was. Rarely does this school get a record broken on Sports Day.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Nor could I, and I was the one running.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: What we need now is a bigger trophy cabinet.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: One step at a time, Liam.

items.sentence: ___ Sofia who organised the whole fundraiser last month.
items.why: an it-cleft in the past, matching 'last month'

items.sentence: Not only ___ the exam, but she also helped her classmates revise.
items.why: 'not only' at the front of a clause triggers subject-auxiliary inversion

items.sentence: ___ have I felt so proud of the whole team.
items.why: 'never before' as a fronted negative adverbial triggers inversion (have + I)

items.sentence: Liam loves hiking in the Andes. ___ does Nadia.
Mateo hasn't finished his essay yet. ___ has Sofia.
___ we need right now is more time to prepare for the mock exam.
items.why: a what-cleft puts 'what we need' as the subject, followed by is/was

practice.instructions: Complete each sentence with one suitable word.

items.sentence: ___ was Liam who forgot to bring the tickets.
___ I need is a quiet place to revise before the exam.
The reason ___ Nadia trains every morning is that she wants to qualify for Nationals.
Not only ___ she win the race, but she also broke the record.
___ have I seen such a well-organised Sports Day.
___ does Miss Vega cancel a lesson — she's very reliable.
Mateo hasn't started revising yet. ___ has Liam.
Sofia loves salsa music. ___ does Nadia.

practice.instructions: Complete the second sentence so that it has a similar meaning to the first. Use the word given. Do not change it. Use between two and five words.

The team didn't only win the match; they also broke the record.
items.second_start: Not only did the team win the match,

items.first: I need a quiet place to revise before the exam, nothing else.
items.second_end: is a quiet place to revise before the exam.

items.first: I have never felt this proud of a team before.
items.second_end: felt this proud of a team.

items.first: Mateo hasn't finished his essay, and Sofia hasn't either.
items.second_start: Mateo hasn't finished his essay, and

summary: Cleft sentences (It was... who, What I need is...) move the important word or idea to the front for emphasis.
'The reason (why)... is' introduces a cause without starting every sentence with 'because'.
'Not only' and negative adverbs like 'never' or 'rarely' at the front of a clause trigger subject-auxiliary inversion.
So/neither/nor + auxiliary + subject shows quick agreement — so for positive statements, neither/nor for negative ones.
None of these structures are compulsory, but using two or three naturally signals a confident, high-level style.
